parts.title: Booking a guided kayak trip
parts.context: A man phones a company to book a family kayak trip.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company to book a guided kayak trip. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Dunmore Kayak Adventures, Fiona speaking.

script.speaker: james
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a guided kayak trip for my family. A colleague of mine did one with you last summer.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Lovely. I'll take a few details, and then I'll tell you about the trips.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants a trip for his family, so 'family' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Can I have your name, please?

script.speaker: james
script.text: It's James Thornley. That's T-H-O-R-N-L-E-Y.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Thank you, Mr Thornley. How many of you will be coming?

script.speaker: james
script.text: There'll be three adults and two children.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: And which day would you like? We have places on Sunday the tenth of August.

script.speaker: james
script.text: That would be perfect. What time does it start?

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: Normally we start at ten, but because of the tides that day, it's nine o'clock. Is that a problem?

script.speaker: james
script.text: Not at all. And where do we meet?

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: At the jetty in Dunmore Bay. It's next to the sailing club, and you'll see our blue van.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: The price is thirty-five pounds for each adult. It was thirty last year, but we've had to put it up. Children are twenty pounds.

script.speaker: james
script.text: That's fine. How old do the children have to be?

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: They must be at least eight. Some companies take younger ones, but we think it's safer to wait. For the longer sea trip they have to be ten, but you've asked for the bay, so eight is enough.

script.speaker: james
script.text: Mine are nine and eleven, so that's all right. What should we bring?

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: A change of clothes, because you will get wet, and a towel. We provide life jackets, and a waterproof bag for your phone and your keys.

script.speaker: james
script.text: That's very helpful. How will I know the booking is confirmed?

script.speaker: fiona
script.text: I'll send a confirmation by email. Please don't expect a text message, because the phone signal in the bay is very poor.

script.speaker: james
script.text: Thanks. I'll look out for it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A talk at a national park
parts.context: A ranger tells visitors where things are and how to behave in a national park.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a park ranger giving a talk to visitors at a national park. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to Ashdale National Park. I'm Tom Ellis, one of the rangers. Please look at the map in your leaflet. We're at the visitor centre, in the middle at the bottom, and the park entrance is just in front of us.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Two main paths start from the junction at the top of the short path ahead of us. If you go straight ahead, at the top of the map, you'll find the viewpoint tower. It's a twenty-minute walk, and from the top you can see the whole valley.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: If you turn left at the junction and walk to the end of the path, close to the lake, you'll find the boat hire. You can borrow a rowing boat for an hour, but you must wear a life jacket.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Turn right instead, and at the far end of that path is the campsite. It's very peaceful, but please book before you go, because it's often full in summer.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Back near the visitor centre, the café is on the left, and it serves hot food until four. On the right of the visitor centre is the picnic area, with tables and a play area for children. The toilets are above the lake path, but the ranger hut, on the edge of the forest, is for staff only.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Now, a few facts and rules. The land was bought for the nation in nineteen fifty-one, but it only became a national park in nineteen seventy-four, after a long campaign by local people.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: We ask you not to fly drones anywhere in the park. People often think the problem is noise, but the real reason is the ospreys. They nest by the lake in spring, and drones frighten the adult birds away from their eggs.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: There are no bins on the paths, so please take your litter home with you. It sounds inconvenient, but the bins used to attract foxes and gulls, and the animals were becoming a problem for the wildlife.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: About the lake. You're welcome to swim, but only in the marked area next to the beach. The water in the middle is deep and very cold, even in July.

script.speaker: ellis
script.text: Finally, on Friday evenings we run a guided night walk, which starts here at eight. You'll see owls, bats and, with luck, a deer. It's free, but you need to bring a torch. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on energy storage
parts.context: Two students plan a presentation on ways of storing renewable energy.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Nadia and Ben, planning a presentation on energy storage. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Ben, we need to decide how to open our presentation on energy storage. I thought we could start with a short video.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: The university's projector is unreliable, though. Last week the sound didn't work at all. I'd rather begin with a question for the audience.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Fine. What kind of question?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: What happens to wind power when the wind stops? That leads straight into our main point, which is that renewable energy needs storage.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Good. How long should the whole thing be? Dr Hughes said twenty minutes.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Twenty minutes including questions, so fifteen for the talk itself. We shouldn't try to cover every technology.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: I've found a great statistic, saying that the amount of storage in the country has doubled in five years.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Be careful. I checked, and it comes from a company's own website, so it might be biased. Use the government report instead.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Right. And the slides? I've put quite a lot of text on each one.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Too much. People can't read and listen at the same time. Use pictures, and no more than twenty words on a slide.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Who should present which part? You're better at the technical bits.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: I'll do the batteries and the hydrogen. You can take the pumped hydro and the conclusion, since you visited the power station.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Let's agree what to say about each method. Lithium batteries first.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: They're very efficient, losing only about ten percent of the energy that goes in. That's their main selling point.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: And pumped hydro?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: It works well, but you need mountains and a lot of water, so not every country can use it.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Hydrogen?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: It's still experimental. There are only a few pilot projects, and nobody knows yet whether it will be competitive.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Compressed air?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Interesting, but it's too expensive. You have to build huge underground caverns, and the cost has stopped most projects.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: And flywheels?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: They're useful for short bursts of power. They react in a fraction of a second, but they can only store energy for a few minutes.

script.speaker: nadia
script.text: Good. That gives us a nice comparison table for the last slide.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Let's practise on Thursday, then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how glaciers form and move
parts.context: A geography lecture on how ice becomes a glacier and how glaciers shape land.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how glaciers form and move. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Glaciers cover about ten percent of the Earth's land surface, and they hold most of the world's fresh water. Today I'd like to explain how they form, and how something so solid can flow.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A glacier begins as snow. Each winter, new snow buries the old, and under the weight, the snow is compressed into small grains of ice. Over many years, these grains are squeezed together, until they become solid ice. In the coldest places, this can take centuries.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Once the ice is about thirty metres thick, it starts to flow under its own weight, like an extremely slow river. This happens in two ways. The first is internal deformation, in which the ice crystals slide over one another. The second is basal sliding. Meltwater at the bottom of the glacier acts as a lubricant, and the whole mass slides over the rock beneath.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Most glaciers move only a few centimetres a day, though some fast-flowing ones can travel tens of metres a day. The surface always moves faster than the base, and the centre faster than the edges, because of the friction with the valley walls.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The top layer of ice is brittle, so when a glacier flows over a bump in the rock, it cracks, and these cracks are called crevasses. They can be dozens of metres deep, and they are dangerous, especially when they are hidden by fresh snow.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: As glaciers move, they reshape the landscape. They pick up rocks, which scrape the valley floor and leave long scratches called striations. When the ice melts, it leaves behind great piles of rock and gravel, known as moraines.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today, most glaciers are shrinking. In the Alps, they have lost about half of their volume since nineteen hundred, and the meltwater is raising sea levels. Next week we'll look at what happens to the water.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
